title: Politics without hatred
hookLine: Hillel and Shammai argue over what to sing to a bride, and the Talmud explains why the gentler house won: an argument for the sake of heaven
tomorrow: a cook was told to add water to the soup. for whom?

lines: WHAT DO YOU SING TO THE BRIDE?
cards: Yard signs go up on the street, and the person two doors down starts to feel like the enemy. The Talmud remembers two schools that disagreed again and again: the house of Hillel and the house of Shammai.
One of their arguments was about a wedding. When you dance in front of the bride, what do you sing about her?

teach.h: SHAMMAI: THE BRIDE AS SHE IS.
teach.b: The house of Shammai said: describe the bride as she is. The Torah says to keep far from falsehood, so you don't call every bride beautiful.
The house of Hillel said: every bride is beautiful and gracious. If a friend comes home from the market with something she bought, do you mock it or praise it? You praise it.
Both sides have a real case. Shammai guards the truth. Hillel guards a person's heart on her wedding day.

teach.h: THESE AND THESE, AND THE GENTLE WIN.
teach.b: Another passage says the two houses argued for three years, each claiming the law followed them, until a voice from heaven said: these and these are the words of the living God, and the law follows the house of Hillel.
Why Hillel? Because they were gentle and humble, and they taught Shammai's words along with their own, even putting Shammai's first.
And the Mishnah says that for all their disputes, the two houses never stopped marrying into each other's families.
That's the Jewish teaching of an argument for the sake of heaven. Pirkei Avot says such an argument will last, and its example is Hillel and Shammai.
The opposite, an argument for its own sake, is Korah's revolt against Moses.
So no hatred doesn't mean no disagreement. It means you can say the other side's best case, and still dance at their wedding.

how: In Jewish study, students learn in pairs (chavruta) and argue over the text, and the Talmud records the losing side's view alongside the winning one. Pirkei Avot's teaching on the argument 'for the sake of heaven' is often quoted to describe how to disagree well.

o: disagreeing hard, honoring the other side
staying out of every political talk

games.q: an argument for heaven: tap the pairs.
p: describe the bride as she is
every bride is beautiful and gracious
both are words of the living God
an argument for its own sake

s: the law followed Hillel because his house had the cleverer arguments
the Talmud says it was because they were gentle and humble, and taught Shammai's view first.
the two houses kept marrying into each other's families
the Mishnah says neither side refused to marry the other's, for all their disputes.
an argument for the sake of heaven is one where both sides end up agreeing
Pirkei Avot says such an argument lasts. the point is how you argue, not that it ends.

games.q: at a family dinner your uncle defends a policy you think is wrong. the house of Hillel's way would have you start by…
o: saying his strongest reason fairly, before your own
letting it drop, since arguing always breeds hatred
listing every flaw in his view so he sees the truth
games.why: Hillel's house taught Shammai's words, even before its own. you can still disagree; you argue for the sake of heaven, not to win.

practice: Bring to mind someone who votes differently from you. Quietly, in a whisper, say the best reason they might give for their view, the way Hillel's house taught Shammai's words first.
Then breathe, and let it sit there without answering it.

wordCard.voice: Politics without hatred: disagreeing hard, for the sake of heaven, the way Hillel's house taught Shammai's words before its own.

orig.note: Hebrew: a dispute. Pirkei Avot speaks of a machloket for the sake of heaven.

carryVoice: Your line: no hatred. Hillel and Shammai argued for years and kept marrying into each other's families. Day 1725, done.

sources.ref: Talmud, Ketubot 16b-17a (how to sing before the bride: Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel)
Talmud, Eruvin 13b (three years of dispute; 'these and these are the words of the living God'; why the law follows Beit Hillel)
Mishnah Yevamot 1:4 (the houses did not refrain from marrying each other's women)
Pirkei Avot 5:17 (a dispute for the sake of heaven will endure: Hillel and Shammai; not for heaven: Korah and his company)
Exodus 23:7 (keep far from a false matter), cited by Beit Shammai
